Chocolate came to Spain from Mexico in the 1500s, after the Spanish conquest of the Aztec lands. Cacao had been grown and drunk in Mesoamerica for thousands of years (cacao first used); the Aztecs drank it cold and bitter, often with chili, and used the beans as money.

The conquistadors around Hernán Cortés saw it at the court of Moctezuma. Cacao travelled to Spain as loaves and tablets that could be stirred into water. The Spanish added sugar, cinnamon and vanilla and drank it hot. By the late 1500s cargoes of cacao came regularly from New Spain to Seville.

For about a century chocolate was mainly a Spanish drink. It then spread to France, Italy and England in the 1600s. With tea and coffee, it was one of three new hot drinks Europe took up in that century, part of the Columbian Exchange. Solid eating chocolate came much later, and milk chocolate only in 1875.
